title: Voice 21
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that Voice 21's oracy programme is a well-intentioned but misguided use of school time, because strong reading and writing are what produce good speakers. He presents himself as ready to be proven wrong and tests the claim against the organisation's own impact report. He finds that the headline outcomes rest on teacher surveys, that the reading gains have no control or comparison group, and that no Progress 8 data is reported. He also notes that the supportive quotes could describe any good teaching, such as cold calling or mini-whiteboards. The piece is a short, sceptical evidence audit of a popular curriculum intervention.
points: The core claim is that oracy follows from reading and writing, so training the speaking itself misses the point.
Salles checks the programme's impact report and finds survey-based outcomes with no counterfactual.
The Voicing Vocabulary result has no comparison group and a self-selected sample, so it cannot show the programme caused the gains.
Testimonials credited to Voice 21 could equally describe ordinary good practice, so they do not isolate its effect.
quotes: But, the thing is, I just don’t believe an Oracy curriculum makes good speakers. Being good at reading and writing makes you a good speaker - you learn how to marshal ideas and evidence into a convincing format which you can then deliver as speech.
Training on the ‘speaky’ part of this misses the point. It is like teaching how to build desirable houses by teaching interior design. Related, but not fundamental.

This appears to have happened in the very first year, and involves around 600 students. Obviously there is no comparison of how previous year groups did in the same schools, or how any control group did in the same cohort. So, you know.

Hmm. More so than actually reading? I mean, you can read 100,000 words of a book much faster than you can practice using 100 new words effectively. Is oracy really going to be more effective than more reading?
I genuinely started this post putting myself on the line, without reading the report. I was 100% prepared to be wrong, in public.
Yes, that is a valid reason to increase Oracy. If other things we value increase, and progress at least doesn’t get worse, then Oracy might be a good bet.
